questions.q: What does the law of unintended consequences describe?
a: Behaviors that appear after an incentive in ways nobody planned
Rewards that work exactly as their designers intended
The habit of ignoring data that contradicts your view
The hidden costs of running a large organization
questions.why: Lesson 1 says incentives always carry side effects that were never part of the plan.

questions.q: How did many Germans respond to less frequent trash pickup and volume-based fees?
a: They dumped rubbish in the woods and flushed food down toilets
They recycled far more carefully than before
They bought smaller bins and started composting
They complained but changed little about their habits
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the waste incentives backfired and people found creative ways around the new system.

questions.q: What does omitted variable bias mean?
a: A key factor has been left out of the analysis
The sample is too small to be reliable
The data covers too short a period of time
A correlation has been mistaken for a cause
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes it as leaving a crucial factor out of your analysis entirely.

questions.q: What actually explained the link between chocolate consumption and Nobel laureates?
a: Wealthier, better-educated countries also buy more luxury foods
Chocolate directly improves brain performance
Nobel winners tend to live in colder climates
The data came from far too few countries
questions.why: Lesson 2 uses the chocolate example to show a hidden factor driving both numbers.

questions.q: Why does the book say you should always collect more data?
a: The most revealing findings only surface in large amounts of it
More data automatically proves a causal relationship
Large datasets remove the need for careful analysis
Surveys are only useful when they reach everyone
questions.why: Lesson 3 says rare and missing data points only appear once you have gathered a great deal.
